subject: Open-Weight Models On The Rise

 Survey Monday 
 
 
 As concerns over AI safety keep mounting, what do you think is the best way to regulate AI? 

 Click here to take the poll and don't forget to share your thoughts in the WSB comments section . 

 
 
 
 
 
    
 
 
 
    
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Good morning! Here's the latest in trending: 

 No deal:  Markets react as Trump rejects  Iran's Hormuz offer , but diplomatic efforts remain active .

 Easing barriers:  U.S. and China agree to tariff cuts for $30B in goods and new coal import deal.

 CAFE reset:  Trump greenlights new fuel economy standards , ending Biden-era EV mandate.
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Top News
 
 
 
 Cutting costs 
 
 
 
Getty Images
 
 
Costs tied to artificial intelligence are soaring , from building the required infrastructure to using the most advanced models in the market. Now, companies are increasingly turning to open-weight AI models over frontier systems of Anthropic ( ANTHRO ) and OpenAI ( OPENAI ) to save on costs.

Dig deeper: Open-weight models are those whose learned parameters are publicly released, allowing users to customize them. Using such models can be cheaper than paying for access to the advanced versions of ChatGPT or Claude. Executive mentions of open models in corporate events increased sixfold in August and September compared with the year-ago period, the Financial Times reported, citing AlphaSense data. For example, PNC ( PNC ) CFO Robert Reilly this month noted that the company is doing its own compute. "We're using the frontier models with the hyperscalers, but we've got open-weight models in our data centers," Reilly said.  C.H. Robinson ( CHRW ) will continue to route simpler workloads to open-source models over time, according to its chief strategy & innovation officer Arun Rajan. "We're very big customers of all the hyperscalers and also using Chinese open-weight models as well to mitigate cost," Match Group ( MTCH ) CEO Spencer Rascoff said. 

"Frontier models like OpenAI's Astra and Claude Fable already have enough intelligence for 90% of the tasks we're trying to do," Vinay Kuruvila, technology chief at Match-owned Tinder, told FT . "If open-weight models catch up, I may not need to use them anymore."  Meanwhile, AT&T ( T ) runs about 40% of its AI workloads on open models and aims to reach 70% within a year, its chief data and AI officer Andy Markus told FT . "The open models are getting better and better. That's giving us more optionality." Besides lower costs, open models also offer sovereignty and security. Data center operator Digital Realty ( DLR ) built its own internal chat interface running on open models. "There's proprietary data we're putting into this private model that I wouldn't put into a frontier model," Scott Wallace, Digital Realty's senior global director of solutions architecture, told FT . "Customer data never, never goes into a frontier."

 Security first:  Nvidia ( NVDA ) just introduced a new open-source tool , Open Agent Safety Platform, designed to strengthen AI security from agent testing through deployment. The platform aims to keep AI agents from going rogue and hacking third-party systems. Companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta ( META ) and Google ( GOOG ) have disclosed breaches by their AI models, prompting industrywide calls for government regulation. OpenAI's recent incidents include breaches of an Australian government system and U.S. government websites, which led to the company pausing training of its latest AI models. OpenAI said it will resume training "only when we are confident that we have additional safeguards" in place. This is the second time in three months that OpenAI halted development of its models, after the Hugging Face hack in July.
